My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, these two items directly contradict each other: being able to talk about the trauma very easily is inconsistent with losing the thread and being unable to finish when trying to explain it. Partial clarity could coexist with fragmented recall, but not with both easy verbal access and marked inability to narrate the event.

vignette: As a park ranger, 32-year-old Kael had always been comfortable in the wilderness, relying on his wits and physical abilities to navigate the rugged terrain. But it was during a brutal interrogation while working abroad that his sense of self-reliance was shattered. Kael's captors had used torture to extract information from him, leaving him with deep-seated fears about his physical vulnerability. In the months following his release, Kael began to notice that he was rehearsing conversations before they happened, mentally preparing himself for every possible scenario in an attempt to regain a sense of control. He would script out what he wanted to say, anticipating potential questions and responses, but this strategy only seemed to heighten his anxiety. His feelings became increasingly numb, as if he had built a wall around himself to prevent any emotional pain from seeping in. Simple tasks like driving or being a passenger in a vehicle triggered a cascade of fears, and Kael found himself avoiding these situations altogether. He would take long detours on foot or bike, preferring the physical exhaustion to the perceived danger of being confined in a car. His colleagues at the park began to notice his changed behavior, but Kael couldn't bring himself to explain why he was no longer willing to participate in routine patrols. Delays of any kind – whether it was waiting for a bus or queuing up for coffee – sent Kael's mind racing with catastrophic scenarios. He would assume that something had gone terribly wrong, and his body would react before his rational thoughts could catch up. His heart would pound, his palms would sweat, and he would scan the surroundings frantically for potential threats. Even in the safety of his own home, Kael found himself repeatedly checking that doors and windows were locked, as if this ritual could somehow ward off the dangers lurking outside. When attempting to recount the events leading up to and during his torture, Kael struggled to articulate what had happened. Some moments stood out with excruciating clarity – the smell of sweat, the sound of screams in the distance – while others remained shrouded in a frustrating fog. He couldn't seem to put the experience into words, as if language itself was insufficient to convey the terror he had endured. Kael's faith in his own resilience had been shattered, and he now questioned whether he could ever rely on anyone else again. His reactions since the event – the hypervigilance, the avoidance behaviors – convinced him that he was losing his grip on reality. The thought sent a chill down his spine: he feared going crazy, succumbing to the very same darkness that had consumed his captors. As Kael navigated his daily routine, these fears and anxieties wove together into a tapestry of dread. He became withdrawn, avoiding social interactions and public spaces where he might be forced to confront his triggers. His work began to suffer as well; once an enthusiastic park ranger, Kael now felt like a shadow of his former self. It was the loss of his job – due in part to his increasing absences and inability to perform routine tasks – that finally prompted Kael to seek help. He knew he couldn't continue living in this state of suspended animation, constantly on edge and unable to shake the feeling of impending doom. With a mix of trepidation and hope, Kael walked into therapy, unsure what lay ahead but desperate for a way out of the darkness that had consumed him.
